Authors

Matthew Ho, Abhiram Gorle, Tsachy Weissman.

Department of Electrical Engineering, Stanford University

How much can a noisy string tell us about a single bit computed from the original? First posed in 2013, the Courtade–Kumar conjecture remained open for more than thirteen years, until the recent proofs in 2026. [1] [10] This post explains our independently developed proof of the Courtade–Kumar conjecture, from the idea behind its induction to the inequalities that required computer assistance.

For a closer look at the mathematics, follow the visual proof map. The In the visual proof links throughout this blog take you directly to the corresponding statements, proofs, and dependencies.

How to read this blog

The Blog tab contains this written walkthrough. Sections 1–3 introduce the problem, place our approach alongside other work, and explain the induction. Sections 4–5 show how the induction step becomes a geometric problem. Sections 6–7 work through its two remaining cases, centered and single-ray, with optional technical derivations for readers who want the calculations. The Visual proof gives the statements and proofs. The Lean certificate writeup explains the certificate families and how they are checked.

1. Introduction: Can a "clever" bit beat a copied one?

Imagine tossing 101 independent fair coins. Before seeing the outcomes, you ask a yes-or-no question about them. Its answer compresses the entire string into a single bit.

Now each coin’s recorded outcome is independently flipped with some fixed probability. An observer receives a noisy version of the original string. They know your question and can use all 101 noisy outcomes to reason about its answer.

Which question should you choose so that the noisy string reveals as much information as possible about the answer?

There are many possibilities:

  • Copy one coordinate: Was the first coin heads?

  • Take a majority: Were more than half the coins heads?

  • Take parity: Was the total number of heads odd?

Copying one coordinate might seem wasteful. Wouldn’t a summary that uses all 101 coins have an advantage over one that ignores 100 of them?

The Courtade–Kumar conjecture [1] proposed a striking answer: no yes-or-no rule can outperform simply copying one coordinate. This holds regardless of the number of coins or the amount of independent noise.

What counts as “outperforming,” though? Suppose your question were: “Did at least one coin land heads?” You could confidently answer “yes” before seeing anything—the chance that all 101 coins landed tails is tiny. You would almost always guess correctly, but that success would have little to do with the noisy observation.

Instead, we ask how much the observation teaches you: how much less uncertain you are about the answer after seeing the noisy string than you were beforehand. This average reduction in uncertainty is what’s called mutual information, and it is what the conjecture compares (Fig. 1).

Nor is this ordinary error correction. We do not get to encode a message into a specially designed pattern before introducing noise. The original coins are independent and fair, and our only choice is which one-bit summary to study.

Finding a rule that achieves the proposed bound is easy: copy a coordinate. The challenge, though, is proving that no seemingly more sophisticated rule can do better, no matter how many coins we toss or how much independent noise we introduce.

Several proofs of this conjecture have now appeared, alongside stronger results and simpler arguments. This post follows our independently developed route1: the idea that made an induction work, the inequalities where the difficulty accumulated, and what computer verification did and did not explain.

Our route

In the visual proofCourtade–Kumar bound ↗

Our approach begins with the uncertainty that remains after seeing the noisy string. Rather than asking only whether the information stays below the coordinate benchmark, we track a more detailed guarantee that depends on how often the Boolean question answers yes.

That extra step makes the induction possible. Fixing one input bit produces two smaller Boolean functions. The task is then to show that their uncertainty guarantees survive the mixing caused by observing that last bit through noise. The proof reduces this task to inequalities involving only a few real parameters, established through analysis and exact certificates. [16]

The starting question is simple: if we already have a useful guarantee for a function of fewer coins, what must that guarantee remember to survive adding one more?

First, let’s place that route alongside the work that came before it.

2. Overview of related work: how we got here

Before the recent proofs

When the conjecture was first posed in 2013, information theory already had a rich body of work analyzing how much information an observation retains after passing through a noisy channel. What those inequalities did not immediately establish was the exact comparison the conjecture needed: no Boolean summary should be more informative than a single coordinate. Obtaining a bound tight enough to establish that comparison was basically the bottleneck. [1] [2] [3]

A lot of the early work studied the conjecture in restricted settings.

One important setting was very noisy observations, where each recorded coin is close to an independent random guess. Early work improved the available bounds for balanced questions: those whose answers are equally likely to be yes or no. A proof subsequently established the conjecture for every Boolean question in a sufficiently noisy range that works regardless of the number of input bits. This independence from the number of bits was important: a noise range that shrinks whenever we enlarge the problem does not give the same guarantee. [4] [5]

Later work substantially enlarged the proved range for balanced questions. Combining analysis with computer-assisted estimates, it established that case whenever the bit-flip probability lies between approximately 4.3% and 50%. But balanced questions are only part of the problem. Even when the input coins are fair, our chosen question might answer yes almost all the time. The full conjecture must therefore cover those questions too. [6]

Some recent work also helped us understand why the observer’s access to the whole noisy string matters. One settled the version where the observer must also compress their observation to a single bit. [7] Another bounded the sum of the information supplied by individual noisy coordinates. [8] Neither directly controls everything the observer might learn by examining those coordinates together: a pattern can reveal something that its individual entries do not.

A further development changed how one could approach the problem. Instead of bounding the information remaining at a particular noise level directly, a differential-equation framework studied how quickly information changes as the noise increases. Controlling that rate and accumulating the control over a range of noise levels offered a route to the desired bound. The framework did not itself complete the conjecture, but it became an important ingredient in subsequent proofs. [9]

Several routes to the same destination

The recent proofs address the remaining challenge: a guarantee covering every Boolean question, every input dimension, and every noise level.

A useful way to understand their differences is to ask: what changes as the proof progresses?

Several arguments follow a function as its observation becomes more or less noisy. One develops a local inequality controlling the rate of information loss [10]. Another combines such estimates with a description of whether the function depends mainly on one coordinate or spreads its dependence across many [11]. A third shows that a hypothetical advantage over a coordinate would have to evolve in a way that contradicts what happens when the noise disappears [12].

Our proof takes a different starting point: hold the noise fixed and build up the number of coordinates. We seek a guarantee for smaller problems that remains valid when they are combined into a larger one. An analytic proof in [13] also followed fixed-noise induction and obtained the same explicit bias-sensitive information bound as ours.

Here, bias-sensitive means that the bound remembers how often the question answers yes. Instead of assigning every Boolean question the same upper limit, it uses that additional information about the question itself.

Keeping the noise fixed does not mean that we avoid calculus. We still use it to prove that our induction step works. Likewise, the proofs that follow changing noise can use induction for some of their intermediate estimates. Fig. 2 compares the two routes by what changes in the outer argument.

Subsequent work also studies randomized one-bit summaries: rules that can use an additional random choice when producing their answer. [14] gives a sharp information-retention bound when the initial amount of information is fixed. It acknowledges that its principal contraction statement also follows from an intermediate result of [10], while developing additional information-loss estimates and an alternative derivation.

Beyond the original question

There has also been recent progress on several closely related questions:

  • Must an almost-optimal rule resemble a copied coordinate? A stability theorem shows that a rule retaining nearly as much information as a coordinate must agree with some coordinate, or its complement, on most inputs. This describes the rule itself, not merely how often it answers yes. [17]

  • What if we retain several bits? Simply copying coordinates can be beaten when the output contains eight or more bits. The proposed optimality statement for two through seven output bits remains conjectural. [12]

  • Can a different measure of distinguishability help? Hellinger inequalities study the overlap between the noisy distributions associated with the two possible answers. Recent work includes a result where the observation is compressed to one bit [18], an analytic result for rules whose answers reverse whenever all input bits are flipped [19], and a manuscript stating the full arbitrary-bias Hellinger inequality [15]. These differ in their assumptions and conclusions, so they should not be treated as interchangeable results.

Comparing the approaches

A certificate provides finite, rigorously checkable evidence for an inequality over an entire region, not merely evaluations at selected points. Lean formalization checks a formal mathematical argument, which can include certificates, analytic reasoning, or both.

The following comparison describes the results and verification records reported in the cited sources.

3. A guarantee that survives one more coin

Suppose we already understand every yes-or-no question about two coins. How could that help us understand a question about three?

Consider majority: did at least two of the three coins land heads?

Imagine fixing the last coin’s original outcome:

  • If it was tails, the answer is yes only when both earlier coins were heads.

  • If it was heads, the answer is yes whenever at least one earlier coin was heads.

One question about three coins has become two questions about two coins.

This works for any Boolean rule, not just majority. Fixing one input leaves two smaller rules. Induction would allow us to work upward from these smaller problems, provided we can show that their guarantees naturally combine into the guarantee needed for the original question.

Throughout this process, the noise stays fixed. If each coin is flipped with probability 10%10\%10%, the smaller problems use that same 10%10\%10%. We change the number of coins, not the channel.

Why it matters how often the answer is yes

There is a useful detail in our majority example.

The original question answers yes half the time. But its two smaller questions do not:

Pr⁡(both coins are heads)=14, and Pr⁡(at least one is heads)=34.\Pr(\text{both coins are heads})=\frac14, \text{ and } \Pr(\text{at least one is heads})=\frac34.Pr(both coins are heads)=41​, and Pr(at least one is heads)=43​.

A question whose answers yes and no are equally likely is called balanced. Even a balanced question can therefore split into unbalanced ones. Other questions can produce a branch whose answer is always yes or always no.

Our induction needs a guarantee that adapts to how often each question answers yes. A fixed positive lower bound on remaining uncertainty could not work: a constant answer has no uncertainty in the first place.

Let XXX denote the string of independent fair coin outcomes, and let fff be our Boolean rule: it returns 111 for yes and 000 for no. Each coordinate is independently flipped with probability α∈[0,1/2]\alpha\in[0,1/2]α∈[0,1/2] to produce the noisy string YYY. U=f(X), and p=Pr⁡(U=1).U=f(X), \text{ and } p=\Pr(U=1).U=f(X), and p=Pr(U=1).

Before seeing the noisy string, our uncertainty about the answer is measured by binary entropy, in bits:

h(t)=−tlog⁡2t−(1−t)log⁡2(1−t), for 0<t<1,h(t)=-t\log_2 t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t), \text{ for }0<t<1,h(t)=−tlog2​t−(1−t)log2​(1−t), for 0<t<1,

We seek a lower bound that depends only on the noise level α\alphaα and the question’s yes-probability ppp:

These checks explain how the formula fits the simplest cases. They do not establish it for an arbitrary question. For that, we must show that it survives the step from two smaller questions to one larger question. [16]

What the observer knows about the smaller questions

Let us make that step precise.

Separate the input into (X′,Z)(X',Z)(X′,Z), where ZZZ is its last coin and X′X'X′ contains all the earlier coins. Fixing ZZZ gives the two smaller rules

p=p0+p12.p=\frac{p_0+p_1}{2}.p=2p0​+p1​​.

qi(y′)=Pr⁡ ⁣(fi(X′)=1∣Y′=y′), for i∈{0,1}.q_i(y') =\Pr\!\bigl(f_i(X')=1|Y'=y'\bigr), \text{ for }i\in\{0,1\}.qi​(y′)=Pr(fi​(X′)=1∣Y′=y′), for i∈{0,1}.

For majority of three, suppose the flip probability is 10%10\%10% and the earlier noisy coins are 0,10,10,1. The first original coin then has a 10%10\%10% chance of being heads, and the second has a 90%90\%90% chance. Consequently:

  • The probability that both were heads is 9%9\%9%.

  • The probability that at least one was heads is 91%91\%91%.

These are the two smaller-question probabilities for this observation.

The induction hypothesis concerns average uncertainty, not the uncertainty after each individual observation. Some observations may leave little doubt about the answer, while others may leave considerably more. The hypothesis states that

E ⁣[h(qi(Y′))]≥Bα(pi), for i=0,1.\mathbb E\!\left[h(q_i(Y'))\right]\ge B_\alpha(p_i), \text{ for }i=0,1.E[h(qi​(Y′))]≥Bα​(pi​), for i=0,1.

On the left, we calculate the uncertainty after each possible observation and then average. On the right, we evaluate the bound at the question’s original yes-probability. Averaging the updated probabilities also recovers the original probability: E[qi(Y′)]=pi\mathbb E[q_i(Y')]=p_iE[qi​(Y′)]=pi​.

The last noisy coin mixes the two possibilities

The observer does not get to see the original last coin ZZZ. They see its noisy version, which we call WWW.

If W=0W=0W=0, the original coin was probably 000, but it could have been 111. Because that original coin was fair, the two probabilities are exactly 1−α1-\alpha1−α and α\alphaα.

So, after a fixed earlier observation y′y'y′, the probability that the whole question answers yes is

r0(y′)=(1−α)q0(y′)+αq1(y′) when W=0.r_0(y') =(1-\alpha)q_0(y')+\alpha q_1(y') \text{ when }W=0.r0​(y′)=(1−α)q0​(y′)+αq1​(y′) when W=0.

r1(y′)=αq0(y′)+(1−α)q1(y′).r_1(y') =\alpha q_0(y')+(1-\alpha)q_1(y').r1​(y′)=αq0​(y′)+(1−α)q1​(y′).

Observing a final noisy 111 instead gives 0.8280.8280.828.

The noisy last coin does not select a branch with certainty. It tells the observer how much weight to give each branch. Fig. 3 shows how those weights change with the observed last coin.

The inequality that makes induction work

In the visual proofBellman inductive hypothesis ↗

We can now calculate the uncertainty remaining about the whole question. The last noisy coin is equally likely to be 000 or 111, independently of the earlier noisy coins. Therefore,

H(U∣Y′,W)=12 E ⁣[h(r0(Y′))+h(r1(Y′))].H(U|Y',W)=\frac12\, \mathbb E\!\left[ h(r_0(Y'))+h(r_1(Y')) \right].H(U∣Y′,W)=21​E[h(r0​(Y′))+h(r1​(Y′))].

To complete the induction step, we need to show that the bounds for the two smaller questions imply

12 E ⁣[h(r0(Y′))+h(r1(Y′))]≥Bα ⁣(p0+p12).\boxed{ \frac12\, \mathbb E\!\left[ h(r_0(Y'))+h(r_1(Y')) \right] \ge B_\alpha\!\left(\frac{p_0+p_1}{2}\right). }21​E[h(r0​(Y′))+h(r1​(Y′))]≥Bα​(2p0​+p1​​).​

The right-hand side is exactly the bound required for the original question, because its yes-probability is (p0+p1)/2(p_0+p_1)/2(p0​+p1​)/2.

This is our mixing theorem: the uncertainty guarantees survive joining the two branches through a noisy last coin. [16]

Why is it not enough simply to average the two smaller guarantees?

Because their average, Bα(p0)+Bα(p1)2\frac{B_\alpha(p_0)+B_\alpha(p_1)}{2}2Bα​(p0​)+Bα​(p1​)​, can be smaller than the required bound for the original question, Bα ⁣(p0+p12)B_\alpha\!\left(\frac{p_0+p_1}{2}\right)Bα​(2p0​+p1​​).

Consider a question that simply copies the last coin. Its two smaller questions are constant: one always answers no, and the other always answers yes. Each has zero uncertainty. Yet the parent must retain h(α)h(\alpha)h(α) bits of uncertainty.

Where does that uncertainty come from? Not knowing which branch the original last coin selected.

For a general question, the mixing theorem must show that this uncertainty about the branch, together with the uncertainty already present within the branches, is enough. Entropy’s concavity helps us obtain a starting bound, but that bound is not yet strong enough.

From one step to every dimension

Once the mixing theorem is established, the induction is straightforward.

With no input coins, every Boolean rule is constant, so the bound holds: both sides are zero. The mixing theorem then carries it from zero coins to one, from one to two, and onward to any number of coins.

Finally, we have

I(U;Y)=h(p)−H(U∣Y).I(U;Y)=h(p)-H(U|Y).I(U;Y)=h(p)−H(U∣Y).

Var⁡(U)=p(1−p).\operatorname{Var}(U)=p(1-p).Var(U)=p(1−p).

The important point is that the stronger bound is not an extra result added after the induction. The more detailed uncertainty bound is what we carry through the induction itself.

We have now seen how the mixing theorem would extend our uncertainty bound to every Boolean function, in any dimension. Next, we turn to proving it. The key is to describe the last mixing step using just a few numbers, rather than analyze every Boolean function separately.

4. Turning the induction step into geometry

The induction has reduced our problem to one question: do the uncertainty bounds for two smaller questions survive their combination through a noisy last coin?

Recall that qi(y′)q_i(y')qi​(y′) is the probability that the smaller question fif_ifi​ answers yes after observing the earlier noisy coins Y′=y′Y'=y'Y′=y′. Section 3 defined this as qi(y′)=Pr⁡(fi(X′)=1∣Y′=y′)q_i(y')=\Pr(f_i(X')=1|Y'=y')qi​(y′)=Pr(fi​(X′)=1∣Y′=y′), for i=0,1i=0,1i=0,1.

For each earlier observation, the effect of the last noisy coin depends only on the probabilities that the two smaller questions answer yes. Different Boolean functions produce different pairs, but the last noisy coin combines them by the same formula.

We therefore look for an inequality that holds for every pair and uses quantities where we can control the averages by induction. We can apply it to each observation and then average, rather than analyze every Boolean function separately. We’ll describe each pair by its midpoint and separation. As we work through the mixing formula below, we’ll see why these are useful quantities to track.

Midpoint and separation

Fix one observation y′y'y′. For the moment, abbreviate q0(y′)q_0(y')q0​(y′) and q1(y′)q_1(y')q1​(y′) to q0q_0q0​ and q1q_1q1​. Instead of tracking them separately, we define

m=q0+q12, and u=∣q1−q0∣2.m=\frac{q_0+q_1}{2}, \text{ and } u=\frac{|q_1-q_0|}{2}.m=2q0​+q1​​, and u=2∣q1​−q0​∣​.

The two probabilities are m−um-um−u and m+um+um+u. For this entropy calculation, their order does not matter: exchanging the branch labels leaves the average entropy unchanged.

We define ρ=1−2α\rho=1-2\alphaρ=1−2α, with 0≤α≤120\le\alpha\le\tfrac120≤α≤21​. The two final probabilities from Section 3, placed in increasing order, are m−ρum-\rho um−ρu and m+ρum+\rho um+ρu. In other words, mixing keeps the midpoint fixed and shrinks the separation by a factor of ρ\rhoρ.

Return to our example with smaller-question probabilities 0.090.090.09 and 0.910.910.91. Their midpoint is 0.50.50.5, and their half-separation is 0.410.410.41. With a flip probability of 0.10.10.1, we have ρ=0.8\rho=0.8ρ=0.8, giving 0.5−0.8(0.41)=0.1720.5-0.8(0.41)=0.1720.5−0.8(0.41)=0.172 and 0.5+0.8(0.41)=0.8280.5+0.8(0.41)=0.8280.5+0.8(0.41)=0.828, exactly the probabilities we calculated in Section 3.

0≤u≤min⁡(m,1−m).0\le u\le\min(m,1-m).0≤u≤min(m,1−m).

This describes the triangle in Fig. 4. Near m=0m=0m=0 or m=1m=1m=1, there is little room for the probabilities to differ, whereas at m=12m=\tfrac12m=21​ their separation can be largest. Every earlier observation gives a point in this triangle. Adding more coins changes which points occur and how often, but not the region containing them. [16]

Two quantities to compare at each point

At a point (m,u)(m,u)(m,u), we define

e(m,u)=h(m−u)+h(m+u)2.e(m,u)=\frac{h(m-u)+h(m+u)}2.e(m,u)=2h(m−u)+h(m+u)​.

This averages the uncertainty within the two smaller questions. It is the remaining uncertainty, for this earlier observation, if the observer is also told the original last coin and therefore knows which branch applies.

In the actual problem, the observer receives only the noisy last coin. We define

jρ(m,u)=h(m−ρu)+h(m+ρu)2.j_\rho(m,u)=\frac{h(m-\rho u)+h(m+\rho u)}2.jρ​(m,u)=2h(m−ρu)+h(m+ρu)​.

This averages the uncertainty after each of the two possible noisy last-coin outcomes. The distinction is about what the observer knows: eee corresponds to knowing the true branch, whereas jρj_\rhojρ​ corresponds to knowing only its noisy indication. We are not comparing uncertainty before and after receiving that indication.

Binary entropy is concave: bringing two probabilities closer together while keeping their midpoint fixed cannot decrease their average entropy. Since mixing replaces m±um\pm um±u by m±ρum\pm\rho um±ρu, we can write

jρ(m,u)≥e(m,u).j_\rho(m,u)\ge e(m,u).jρ​(m,u)≥e(m,u).

This gives a first comparison, but it does not yet give the lower bound Bα(p)B_\alpha(p)Bα​(p) that we will need after averaging. We'll therefore need to quantify the entropy increase more precisely.

Letting Y′Y'Y′ vary makes mmm and uuu random. Averaging over those earlier observations recovers the quantity we want to bound:

E[jρ(m,u)]=H(U∣Y′,W).\mathbb E\bigl[j_\rho(m,u)\bigr]=H(U|Y',W).E[jρ​(m,u)]=H(U∣Y′,W).

We can picture jρj_\rhojρ​ as the height of a surface above the triangle. The mixing theorem asks for a lower bound on its average height over the points generated by our observations.

What does induction tell us?

The mean midpoint is still the original question's yes-probability:

E[m]=p0+p12=p.\mathbb E[m]=\frac{p_0+p_1}{2}=p.E[m]=2p0​+p1​​=p.

There is a subtlety here. We sorted the probabilities separately at each observation. The smaller one might come from branch 000 for one observation and branch 111 for another. Consequently, p−dp-dp−d and p+dp+dp+d need not be the original branch probabilities p0p_0p0​ and p1p_1p1​. We cannot simply apply the induction hypothesis separately to the two sorted quantities.

However, we can still bound the average uncertainty across the two branches. Sorting does not change the sum of their entropy terms, so the two induction hypotheses give

E[e(m,u)]≥Bα(p0)+Bα(p1)2.\mathbb E[e(m,u)]\ge\frac{B_\alpha(p_0)+B_\alpha(p_1)}2.E[e(m,u)]≥2Bα​(p0​)+Bα​(p1​)​.

To express this bound using our new coordinates, observe that p0p_0p0​ and p1p_1p1​ both lie between p−dp-dp−d and p+dp+dp+d: indeed, 2d=E∣q1−q0∣≥∣p1−p0∣2d=\mathbb E|q_1-q_0|\ge|p_1-p_0|2d=E∣q1​−q0​∣≥∣p1​−p0​∣. Both pairs have midpoint ppp, so the new pair is at least as spread out as the original pair. Because BαB_\alphaBα​ is concave, spreading a pair farther apart without changing its midpoint cannot increase the average of its two values. Therefore,

Bα(p0)+Bα(p1)2≥Bα(p−d)+Bα(p+d)2.\frac{B_\alpha(p_0)+B_\alpha(p_1)}2 \ge \frac{B_\alpha(p-d)+B_\alpha(p+d)}2.2Bα​(p0​)+Bα​(p1​)​≥2Bα​(p−d)+Bα​(p+d)​.

We define the last expression as EreqE_{\mathrm{req}}Ereq​. We now have three pieces of information:

E[m]=p and E[u]=d,   with   E[e(m,u)]≥Ereq,\mathbb E[m]=p \text{ and } \mathbb E[u]=d, \;\text{ with }\; \mathbb E[e(m,u)]\ge E_{\mathrm{req}},E[m]=p and E[u]=d, with E[e(m,u)]≥Ereq​,

Ereq=Bα(p−d)+Bα(p+d)2.E_{\mathrm{req}}=\frac{B_\alpha(p-d)+B_\alpha(p+d)}2.Ereq​=2Bα​(p−d)+Bα​(p+d)​.

These averages do not tell us which points occur or how frequently: different Boolean questions can produce different distributions of points. Rather than recover that function-specific detail, we prove that the three constraints above are enough. An inequality valid at every point of the triangle can then be averaged over any of those distributions. This is why the reduction can cover every Boolean question without analyzing its observations one by one. [16]

How can we use these averages?

The central idea is to bound the difficult quantity using quantities whose averages we can control.

We seek constants θ≥0\theta\ge0θ≥0, aaa, and bbb such that the following inequality holds throughout that triangle:

θEreq+ap+bd≥Bα(p).(B)\boxed{\theta E_{\mathrm{req}}+ap+bd\ge B_\alpha(p).} \tag{B}θEreq​+ap+bd≥Bα​(p).​(B)

The next part of the proof constructs these bounds by studying where a plane can meet the adjusted surface without crossing above it. That analysis leads to the configurations we call centered and single-ray, with boundary cases treated separately. [16]

5. From supporting planes to the centered and single-ray cases

Section 4 leaves us with two things to establish: the plane must stay below the adjusted entropy surface everywhere, and its averaged bound must reach Bα(p)B_\alpha(p)Bα​(p).

How do we find such a plane?

The basic idea is to look for where the bound becomes tight. Those contact points describe a much simpler distribution of probability pairs, which we will call our comparison distribution. Instead of tracking all the posterior probabilities generated by a Boolean function, we will need to understand just a few carefully chosen pairs.

Choosing the comparison distribution

From Section 4, we know that

E[m]=p and E[u]=d, with E[e(m,u)]≥Ereq.\mathbb E[m]=p\text{ and } \mathbb E[u]=d,\text{ with } \mathbb E[e(m,u)]\ge E_{\mathrm{req}}.E[m]=p and E[u]=d, with E[e(m,u)]≥Ereq​.

We seek a comparison distribution with the same means p,dp,dp,d but with average branch entropy exactly EreqE_{\mathrm{req}}Ereq​. Its remaining entropy after mixing should be no greater than that of our original distribution.

If we can prove the required lower bound even for this comparison, the original distribution must satisfy it too.

We choose the comparison directly from probability pairs and their weights, without requiring it to come from another Boolean function. Its pairs are contact points where the supporting-plane bound is exact, and its weights give the means p,dp,dp,d and average branch entropy EreqE_{\mathrm{req}}Ereq​.

Let's consider 0<α<120<\alpha<\tfrac120<α<21​ and 0<d<p≤120<d<p\le\tfrac120<d<p≤21​. We can assume p≤12p\le\tfrac12p≤21​ by exchanging the labels “yes” and “no,” which leaves entropy unchanged. The excluded boundary cases are handled separately.

From a surface to a curve

At a point with m>0m>0m>0, define the relative separation r=u/mr=u/mr=u/m. Then u=rmu=rmu=rm, and the two sorted probabilities are m(1−r)m(1-r)m(1−r) and m(1+r)m(1+r)m(1+r).

Doubling the branch probabilities from (0.1,0.3)(0.1,0.3)(0.1,0.3) to (0.2,0.6)(0.2,0.6)(0.2,0.6) also doubles their midpoint, from 0.20.20.2 to 0.40.40.4, and their half-separation, from 0.10.10.1 to 0.20.20.2. Their ratio r=u/mr=u/mr=u/m stays at 1/21/21/2. Thus both (m,u)(m,u)(m,u) points lie on the same line u=m/2u=m/2u=m/2 through the origin.

We do this because, along that direction, the plane inequality becomes

jρ(m,rm)−θe(m,rm)m≥a+br.\frac{j_\rho(m,rm)-\theta e(m,rm)}{m} \ge a+br.mjρ​(m,rm)−θe(m,rm)​≥a+br.

The right-hand side no longer depends on mmm. To make the inequality hold along the entire direction, we therefore need to find the smallest value of the left-hand side.

For a fixed 0<θ<10<\theta<10<θ<1, define

cθ(r)=min⁡0<m≤1/(1+r)jρ(m,rm)−θe(m,rm)m.c_\theta(r)= \min_{0<m\le 1/(1+r)} \frac{j_\rho(m,rm)-\theta e(m,rm)}{m}.cθ​(r)=0<m≤1/(1+r)min​mjρ​(m,rm)−θe(m,rm)​.

The upper limit simply ensures that the larger probability, m(1+r)m(1+r)m(1+r), does not exceed one.

Dividing by mmm lets us work with a curve instead of the two-variable surface. We need to find a straight line a+bra+bra+br that stays below cθ(r)c_\theta(r)cθ​(r). Multiplying by mmm then gives the plane we need.

A straight segment and a convex branch

In the visual proofConvex-envelope formula ↗

The curve cθc_\thetacθ​ need not itself be convex. Instead, consider the highest convex curve that lies below it. Convexity matters because a supporting line to that lower curve stays below it everywhere and therefore below the original curve.

Our proof shows that this lower curve has two parts:

  • First comes a straight segment, from r=0r=0r=0 to a transition point r=r∗r=r_*r=r∗​.

  • After that comes a curved, strictly convex branch that follows cθc_\thetacθ​ itself.

At the transition, the minimizing point in the original triangle has midpoint m=12m=\tfrac12m=21​.

Our proof establishes this shape using the specific properties of binary entropy. We find a unique minimizing point along each nonzero direction, prove positive curvature on the relevant branch, and use the symmetry between yes and no to show that the straight segment stays below the entire profile. We prove these properties analytically. The numerical certificates enter later, when we establish the centered and single-ray inequalities. [16]

The averages ppp and ddd tell us where the line needs to touch the curve. We define rˉ=d/p\bar r=d/prˉ=d/p. Averaging a plane gives ap+bd=p(a+brˉ)ap+bd=p(a+b\bar r)ap+bd=p(a+brˉ), so only the supporting line's value at rˉ\bar rrˉ enters our bound. We therefore choose a line that touches the lower curve there: on the straight segment this gives centered, while on the curved branch it gives single-ray (Fig. 6).

Here rˉ\bar rrˉ is the ratio of the two means, not necessarily the average of the individual ratios u/mu/mu/m.

Matching the branch entropy

In the visual proofTwo-phase support theorem ↗

There is still a parameter to choose: θ\thetaθ, the coefficient of the inherited entropy term.

Changing θ\thetaθ changes the adjusted surface and moves its contact points. For the constraints arising here, our geometric argument proves that a suitable choice produces a comparison distribution with average branch entropy exactly EreqE_{\mathrm{req}}Ereq​ and with nonnegative weights summing to one. We call this equality the entropy-matching condition.

We can now describe the resulting distributions explicitly.

Centered configuration: one symmetric uncertain pair and certain answers

The centered comparison uses three possible pairs of branch probabilities:

  • (0,0)(0,0)(0,0): both branches certainly answer no.

  • (1,1)(1,1)(1,1): both branches certainly answer yes.

  • ((1−r)/2,(1+r)/2)\bigl((1-r)/2,(1+r)/2\bigr)((1−r)/2,(1+r)/2): one uncertain pair symmetric about 12\tfrac1221​.

Here rrr describes the separation within the uncertain pair, and it need not equal the overall ratio d/pd/pd/p. Let www be the probability assigned to that pair. Its half-separation is r/2r/2r/2, so its weight connects the two through wr/2=dwr/2=dwr/2=d.

The other two weights are 1−p−w/21-p-w/21−p−w/2 and p−w/2p-w/2p−w/2. Together, these choices give the required mean midpoint ppp. Only the uncertain pair contributes entropy, since the two certain pairs remain certain after mixing. Entropy matching therefore gives

w h ⁣(1−r2)=Ereq.w\,h\!\left(\frac{1-r}{2}\right)=E_{\mathrm{req}}.wh(21−r​)=Ereq​.

Noise shrinks the uncertain pair's separation from rrr to ρr\rho rρr. Consequently, the comparison's remaining entropy is

Jcentered=w h ⁣(1−ρr2).J_{\mathrm{centered}}= w\,h\!\left(\frac{1-\rho r}{2}\right).Jcentered​=wh(21−ρr​).

The supporting-plane argument proves that the original distribution has at least this much remaining entropy. The separate centered inequality must then establish

Jcentered≥Bα(p).J_{\mathrm{centered}}\ge B_\alpha(p).Jcentered​≥Bα​(p).

Importantly, the uncertain pair is centered, but the overall question need not be balanced. Unequal weights on the certain-no and certain-yes pairs allow the overall probability ppp to differ from 12\tfrac1221​.

Single-ray configuration: one uncertain pair and a certain answer

On the curved branch, the comparison has an even smaller collection of possibilities:

  • The certain-no pair (0,0)(0,0)(0,0).

  • One uncertain pair (z(1−r),z(1+r))\bigl(z(1-r),z(1+r)\bigr)(z(1−r),z(1+r)).

Here zzz is the uncertain pair's midpoint, and r=d/pr=d/pr=d/p. Assigning probability p/zp/zp/z to that pair gives mean midpoint ppp and mean half-separation pr=dpr=dpr=d. The remaining probability is assigned to (0,0)(0,0)(0,0).

The chosen contact satisfies p≤z≤12p\le z\le\tfrac12p≤z≤21​, so p/zp/zp/z really is a probability. Entropy matching takes the form

pz e(z,rz)=Ereq.\frac pz\,e(z,rz)=E_{\mathrm{req}}.zp​e(z,rz)=Ereq​.

The comparison's remaining entropy is

Jray=pz jρ(z,rz).J_{\mathrm{ray}}=\frac pz\,j_\rho(z,rz).Jray​=zp​jρ​(z,rz).

Again, the support gives a lower bound for the original distribution, and a separate inequality must prove

Jray≥Bα(p).J_{\mathrm{ray}}\ge B_\alpha(p).Jray​≥Bα​(p).

Unlike the centered configuration's uncertain pair, this pair is generally not centered at 12\tfrac1221​. Both its location and its separation matter.

The two descriptions fit together at their shared boundary. There, z=12z=\tfrac12z=21​, and the centered configuration's weight on the certain-yes pair becomes zero. The centered and single-ray comparison distributions then coincide.

Back to the original question

The comparison points were chosen where the supporting plane is tight. Their means match p,dp,dp,d, and their average branch entropy equals EreqE_{\mathrm{req}}Ereq​. Therefore, the lower bound from Section 4 becomes exactly their remaining entropy:

Eoriginal[jρ]≥θEreq+ap+bd=Jcomparison.\mathbb E_{\mathrm{original}}[j_\rho] \ge \theta E_{\mathrm{req}}+ap+bd= J_{\mathrm{comparison}}.Eoriginal​[jρ​]≥θEreq​+ap+bd=Jcomparison​.

This inequality shows why we can use the simpler distribution: any lower bound we prove for its remaining entropy also holds for the original distribution.

We have therefore separated the problem into two parts. The geometry identifies simple comparison distributions and proves that they give lower bounds for all the original ones. The centered and single-ray inequalities must then show that those lower bounds reach Bα(p)B_\alpha(p)Bα​(p).

What remains is to prove the required bound for each comparison. We start with the centered case, explaining how symmetry simplifies the calculation and where the positivity certificate for the centered inequality is used.

6. The centered inequality

In the visual proofCentered inequality ↗

In the centered case, only one pair in our comparison distribution contributes any entropy. With probability www, the two branch probabilities are (1−r)/2(1-r)/2(1−r)/2 and (1+r)/2(1+r)/2(1+r)/2. w h ⁣(1−ρr2)≥Bα(p).\boxed{w\,h\!\left(\frac{1-\rho r}{2}\right)\ge B_\alpha(p).}wh(21−ρr​)≥Bα​(p).​

D(p,a)=h(p)−h(p−a)+h(p+a)2, for p−a,p+a∈[0,1].D(p,a)=h(p)-\frac{h(p-a)+h(p+a)}2, \text{ for }p-a,p+a\in[0,1].D(p,a)=h(p)−2h(p−a)+h(p+a)​, for p−a,p+a∈[0,1].

In the visual proofUpper bound for the weight ↗

We still need to use an important restriction on www: entropy matching does not allow it to range freely over the whole unit interval.

For fixed w,rw,rw,r, the average of Bα(p−wr/2)B_\alpha(p-wr/2)Bα​(p−wr/2) and Bα(p+wr/2)B_\alpha(p+wr/2)Bα​(p+wr/2) is largest when p=1/2p=1/2p=1/2. This follows from the symmetry and concavity of BαB_\alphaBα​.

Consider the weight wbw_bwb​ that makes entropy matching hold at this balanced mean:

wb h ⁣(1−r2)=Bα ⁣(1−wbr2).w_b\,h\!\left(\frac{1-r}{2}\right) =B_\alpha\!\left(\frac{1-w_b r}{2}\right).wb​h(21−r​)=Bα​(21−wb​r​).

There is exactly one such weight in (0,1)(0,1)(0,1). As the weight increases, the left-hand side increases while the right-hand side decreases, and their ordering reverses between the endpoints.

Every entropy-matched centered comparison satisfies w≤wbw\le w_bw≤wb​, so the balanced case bounds the uncertain weight even when the original question is unbalanced. We can replace the implicitly defined wbw_bwb​ with an explicit upper bound, which we call the cap:

w≤wb≤A(R,r), where A(R,r)=1−R1−Rr2.\boxed{ w\le w_b\le A(R,r), \text{ where } A(R,r)=\sqrt{\frac{1-R}{1-Rr^2}}. }w≤wb​≤A(R,r), where A(R,r)=1−Rr21−R​​.​

At w=A(R,r)w=A(R,r)w=A(R,r), a calculus estimate shows that the left-hand side of the balanced matching equation is at least as large as the right-hand side. Since their difference increases with www, its zero lies at or below A(R,r)A(R,r)A(R,r). [16]

Checking the bound at the cap

An upper bound on www would be useful only if we know how our lower bound changes with www. Divide TTT by a positive factor and define

Q(R,w,r)=T(w,r)(1−R)wr2.Q(R,w,r)=\frac{T(w,r)}{(1-R)wr^2}.Q(R,w,r)=(1−R)wr2T(w,r)​.

This changes the scale but not the sign. More importantly, direct differentiation shows that QQQ decreases as www increases, with RRR and rrr held fixed. This monotonicity holds throughout 0<w<10<w<10<w<1, not just at entropy-matched weights.

Therefore,

Q(R,w,r)≥Q(R,A(R,r),r).Q(R,w,r)\ge Q\bigl(R,A(R,r),r\bigr).Q(R,w,r)≥Q(R,A(R,r),r).

Q(R,A(R,r),r)≥0.\boxed{Q\bigl(R,A(R,r),r\bigr)\ge0.}Q(R,A(R,r),r)≥0.​

Onto the computer-assisted proof

In the visual proofPositivity certificate for the centered inequality ↗Extension to all allowed weights ↗

To prove this inequality, we follow QQQ along the cap as its weight and the channel parameter vary together. We vary the channel only for this scalar calculation, while the induction itself still keeps the noise fixed. Because QQQ approaches zero at the completely noisy endpoint (R→0R\to0R→0), it suffices to bound its derivative along the cap and show that moving away from that endpoint keeps the expression nonnegative.

Follow the derivative along the centered cap

To make this precise, keep rrr fixed and use ccc for the weight along the cap. Rearranging the cap equation gives R=(1−c2)/(1−c2r2)R=(1-c^2)/(1-c^2r^2)R=(1−c2)/(1−c2r2). Define

Fr(c)=Q ⁣(1−c21−c2r2, c, r).F_r(c)=Q\!\left(\frac{1-c^2}{1-c^2r^2},\,c,\,r\right).Fr​(c)=Q(1−c2r21−c2​,c,r).

This is our expression evaluated along the cap. In particular, at c=A(R,r)c=A(R,r)c=A(R,r) it equals the quantity we need to bound. It approaches zero as ccc approaches 111, so we define its endpoint value as Fr(1)=0F_r(1)=0Fr​(1)=0.

If we establish −Fr′(c)≥0-F_r'(c)\ge0−Fr′​(c)≥0 throughout 0<c<10<c<10<c<1, integration gives

Fr(c)=∫c1[−Fr′(t)] dt≥0.F_r(c)=\int_c^1[-F_r'(t)]\,dt\ge0.Fr​(c)=∫c1​[−Fr′​(t)]dt≥0.

The endpoint integral is understood as a limit. We vary the channel here only to prove the scalar inequality, while the outer induction continues to use a fixed noise level.

The quantity we need to prove nonnegative still contains logarithms, so we first bound it from below using analytic estimates. Truncating a series with nonnegative terms provides one such bound, since its omitted tail is nonnegative. After changing coordinates and clearing a denominator that is positive in the interior, it suffices to show that the resulting polynomial is nonnegative on the unit square.

The positivity certificate for the centered inequality proves that this polynomial is nonnegative using an exact Bernstein expansion. Its basis functions are products of one-variable terms of the form (ni)ti(1−t)n−i\binom{n}{i} t^i(1-t)^{n-i}(in​)ti(1−t)n−i, which are nonnegative on 0≤t≤10\le t\le10≤t≤1. Their products are therefore nonnegative throughout the unit square.

The expansion has 2,928 rational coefficients, and we verify two facts:

  1. The expansion equals the intended polynomial exactly.

  2. Every coefficient is nonnegative.

Together, these checks prove that every term in the sum, and therefore the polynomial itself, is nonnegative throughout the square (Fig. 9).

This proves the required derivative bound along the cap. Integrating from the completely noisy endpoint gives Q(R,A(R,r),r)≥0Q(R,A(R,r),r)\ge0Q(R,A(R,r),r)≥0. [16]

The cap bound gives Q(R,w,r)≥0Q(R,w,r)\ge0Q(R,w,r)≥0 and hence T(w,r)≥0T(w,r)\ge0T(w,r)≥0 for every allowed centered comparison. Its remaining entropy is therefore at least Bα(p)B_\alpha(p)Bα​(p), and the supporting-plane argument transfers that bound to the original distribution. Next we turn to the single-ray case, where the uncertain pair need not be centered at 1/21/21/2.

7. The single-ray inequality

Unlike the centered case, where the uncertain pair is centered at 1/21/21/2, the single-ray case allows the pair's center to move, so the entropy gained from contracting its separation depends on where the pair sits.

Recall from Section 5 that the single-ray comparison places probability p/zp/zp/z on the uncertain pair (z(1−r),z(1+r))(z(1-r),z(1+r))(z(1−r),z(1+r)) and the remaining probability on (0,0)(0,0)(0,0), where ppp is the overall mean and zzz is the pair's center. In the single-ray case, the comparison lies along one direction, so its relative separation is r=d/pr=d/pr=d/p. We treat the interior case 0<p≤z<1/20<p\le z<1/20<p≤z<1/2 and 0<r<10<r<10<r<1 here, and since p≤zp\le zp≤z, the weight p/zp/zp/z is a valid probability that preserves the mean ppp.

Onto the computer-assisted proof

In the visual proofPositivity certificates for t2≤17/20t^2\le17/20t2≤17/20 ↗Nonnegativity at Mc=v/(1+v)M_c=v/(1+v)Mc​=v/(1+v) ↗Nonnegativity at the midpoint ↗A determinant bound for ℓ(M)−ℓ(Mc)\ell(M)-\ell(M_c)ℓ(M)−ℓ(Mc​) ↗

Establishing S′(R)≥0S'(R)\ge0S′(R)≥0 across the single-ray parameter space requires several types of estimates:

  • Series and calculus regimes: In parts of the domain, direct calculus and entropy comparisons suffice. In others, we expand the expression into a convergent series, using the positivity certificates for t2≤17/20t^2\le17/20t2≤17/20 for a finite number of initial terms and an analytic bound for the remaining tail.

  • Rigorous box subdivision: Elsewhere, we partition the parameter range into small boxes and compute a lower bound valid across each box, accounting for both rounding and logarithm-approximation errors. The certificates for nonnegativity at Mc=v/(1+v)M_c=v/(1+v)Mc​=v/(1+v) and certificates for nonnegativity at the midpoint use bounds of this kind. A box passes if its lower bound is nonnegative. A lower bound below zero does not refute the inequality but leaves the box uncertified. We then sharpen the estimate or subdivide the box. The certified boxes and analytic estimates must cover the whole required region, and a box can be omitted only after proving that it contains no admissible parameters.

  • Near-noiseless cancellation and limit: Close to the noiseless channel (R→1R\to1R→1), positive and negative terms nearly cancel. Rather than bounding them separately, the proof of the determinant bound for ℓ(M)−ℓ(Mc)\ell(M)-\ell(M_c)ℓ(M)−ℓ(Mc​) groups the potentially negative term with the positive target-gap contribution and certifies a bound on their combination, with analytic error estimates justifying the simplifications. Finally, to cover channels arbitrarily close to R=1R=1R=1 without leaving an untreated gap, an analytic estimate identifies the leading expression as R→1R\to1R→1, bounds the remaining error, and overlaps with the regions covered by finite certificates. [16]

Fig. 12 illustrates these verification tools, not consecutive intervals of the noise parameter. Their applicability also depends on the other parameters, and together with the analytic reductions they cover every admissible case.

Return to the induction step

Since S(0)=0S(0)=0S(0)=0 and S′(R)≥0S'(R)\ge0S′(R)≥0, we have S(Rf)≥0S(R_{\mathrm f})\ge0S(Rf​)≥0 at the target channel, giving Er(m∗)/m∗≤Er(z)/zE_r(m_*)/m_*\le E_r(z)/zEr​(m∗​)/m∗​≤Er​(z)/z. Because both before- and after-mixing entropy ratios decrease with the center location, this implies z≤m∗z\le m_*z≤m∗​ and hence

pzEρr(z)≥pm∗Eρr(m∗)=Bα(p).\frac pz E_{\rho r}(z) \ge\frac p{m_*}E_{\rho r}(m_*) =B_\alpha(p).zp​Eρr​(z)≥m∗​p​Eρr​(m∗​)=Bα​(p).

The boundary cases are handled without dividing by zero: centered comparisons (z=1/2z=1/2z=1/2) belong to the centered case, full separation (r=1r=1r=1) follows by continuity, and zero separation (r=0r=0r=0) along with the extreme noise levels (R∈{0,1}R\in\{0,1\}R∈{0,1}) follow from direct entropy identities.

The supporting-plane argument transfers this bound to the original distribution. Together, the centered and single-ray inequalities establish the mixing theorem, so the fixed-channel induction gives H(U∣Y)≥Bα(p)H(U|Y)\ge B_\alpha(p)H(U∣Y)≥Bα​(p) in every dimension and hence the bias-sensitive information bound from Section 3.

  • Section 3, induction: uncertainty envelope and mixing statement, fixed-channel induction.

  • Section 4, mixing and support: combined entropy constraint, ordered-triangle reduction, averaging a global support.

  • Section 5, centered and single-ray configurations: radial contacts, global chord, two support configurations.

  • Section 6, centered inequality: entropy-drop reduction, balanced-contact cap, positivity certificate data for the centered inequality, Centered inequality in bits.

  • Section 7, single-ray inequality: flow identities, global flow integration, certificate assembly for nonnegativity at the endpoint, assembly for the remaining near-noiseless region, full flow assembly.

The authors drew inspiration for this blog’s layout and presentation from Hyperstition’s blogs.
